detail.abstract: Synthetic datasets, simulation systems, and test-data generators are established, and prior work has already described synthetic datasets as data products. This paper therefore does not claim novelty in synthetic generation itself. It proposes a narrower theoretical construct: the generative data product (GDP), a distinct subclass of data product in which the persistent product object is a governed, versioned capability for repeatedly generating fit-for-purpose data instances from an executable generative specification. The defining productive sequence is knowledge and specification → generative capability → data. The executable specification may encode domain models, schemas, standards, business rules, constraints, distributions, learned statistical representations, scenarios, validation suites, and delivery requirements. Some GDPs can be source-independent, while others can be source-informed through models learned from empirical data. In either case, the durable product is not reducible to one generated dataset. This distinguishes the GDP from source data products that curate observations, derived products that transform existing data, and analytical products that infer scores or insights from data. The paper develops the Werkstatt Model to explain the product form and lifecycle of this capability. The workshop metaphor emphasizes making, inspection, adaptation, maintenance, and repair. Two supporting constructs are specified: operational fidelity, the degree to which generated data satisfy the structures, rules, relationships, scenarios, interfaces, and other requirements of a declared operational purpose; and generation lineage, a GDP-specific provenance profile that records the generative conditions under which an instance was produced. Enterprise data operations provide the principal scope of analysis, including software testing, migration, integration, modernization, interoperability, performance testing, training, and development. Five propositions connect product persistence, knowledge substitution, scarcity migration, operational fidelity, and maintenance capability. The central theoretical implication is that a data product need not begin with empirical data. Under appropriate conditions, executable knowledge and specification can become productive inputs from which governed data instances are generated. As those instances become inexpensive to reproduce, durable value can migrate toward domain knowledge, validation authority, governance, and maintenance capacity.

title: Too Smart to Last: The AI Capability Paradox on Corpus Commons

detail.title: Too Smart to Last: The AI Capability Paradox on Corpus Commons
detail.abstract: Generative AI depends on human-generated data, yet greater AI capability also changes creators’ incentives to produce the original content on which future AI models rely. We study this feedback through a dynamic model of corpus commons in which strategic creators choose between original human production and AI-derivative production, while semantic coverage of AI models and the derivative share of the corpus co-evolve over time. We establish conditions for uniqueness and global convergence and show how stronger attention congestion and more responsive, or less diverse, creators can instead generate multiple stationary regimes and tipping. We then identify an AI capability paradox: greater capability can crowd out original production, thereby increasing the derivative share of the corpus, weakening semantic renewal, and ultimately reducing long-run coverage. Better filtering or provenance can similarly backfire when the induced substitution toward derivative production is sufficiently strong. Sufficiently large technical improvements can even eliminate a high-coverage regime and trigger a discontinuous transition to a low-coverage outcome. Finally, we characterize policies for sustaining the corpus commons. State-contingent originality incentives can implement desired corpus targets, while the long-run and intertemporal optima account for the value of semantic renewal and the displacement of derivative inflow. The results show that technical improvements and creator incentives should be complements in sustaining the corpus on which generative AI depends.

detail.abstract:
Motivation: Resource-rich economies are often assessed through endowments, export prospects and project announcements. Development policy also needs to explain how national priorities, institutional capabilities and public-finance instruments are translated into implementable investment and durable domestic value.
Purpose: This article develops developmental bankability and uses Japan-Algeria cooperation as a bounded, collaborative case to examine project-level governance linking enabling policy, external capabilities, public finance and quality foreign direct investment (FDI).
Approach and Methods: An embedded single-case design with structured documentary analysis covers January 2022 to 14 July 2026, supplemented by foundational literature and the Sahara Solar Breeder/Sahara Solar Energy Research Center (SSB/SSERC) cooperation precedent. Evidence is coded around ownership, payment, technical readiness, O&M, risk, additionality and FDI-quality effects.
Findings: Algeria's investment momentum and policy initiatives provide a constructive basis for cooperation. The case differentiates modular service entry points, structured system-level preparation and coordination-intensive pathways. SSB/SSERC shows how sustained pre-commercial research and capability formation can create institutional learning that supports later preparation without itself demonstrating commercial bankability. Across pathways, project-level governance is strengthened when ownership, payment, operating responsibility, risk and expected domestic-value outcomes are jointly specified.
Policy Implications: A jointly owned PAUSE, REFINE and ADVANCE framework can reduce cross-organisational coordination costs by making evidence states, responsibilities and next preparation tasks explicit. Embedding the gates in public-investment and external development-finance procedures connects the enabling economic-policy environment with appraisal, instrument choice and ex-post learning.

detail.abstract: A human-AI team can perform poorly even when both members are capable, because team performance depends on how work is allocated as well as on who is available. We develop the Delegation Efficient Frontier (DEF) to evaluate an observed delegation rule relative to the best outcome attainable from the same candidates, assignment-time information, decision right or implemented-action proxy, constraints, population, and outcome definition. Its authority-quality curve traces maximal quality over AI-use shares and separates three margins: the amount of AI use, the information available for assignment, and task-level placement. Portfolio, multi-moment, and distributional representations extend the framework to correlated workflow performance, multiple organizational objectives, and complete outcome laws. To demonstrate how the DEF can be constructed empirically, we use a public AI-assisted chess experiment with 100 participants and 3,000 decisions. The dataset records the participant's initial move, the AI recommendation, the quality of both candidate moves, information available before the final choice, and the implemented action. On 2,571 eligible trials, repeated participant-level cross-fitting estimates predictable AI-human comparative advantage and traces the attainable quality frontier over different AI-action shares. At the observed 49.6-percent share, recorded quality is 42.5 percent, while the system-information and history-only frontiers reach 63.5 and 41.5 percent, respectively. These comparisons illustrate the diagnostic value of the DEF: it distinguishes performance associated with information-set expansion from placement within a fixed information set.

title: Individuals as Perceptual Entities: A Developmental Typology Under Premise-Shifting Change
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Individuals as Perceptual Entities: A Developmental Typology Under Premise-Shifting Change
detail.abstract: Existing developmental traditions, including Erikson, Kegan, Seligman, terror management theory, and attachment theory, each specify development from within the meaning frameworks individuals inhabit. None specifies the prior mechanism: why those frameworks generate their own limits, what structural conditions individuals bring to each transition, and what enables reconstruction. Premise-shifting change, the recurring displacement of governing premises organizing entire domains of expertise, identity, and meaning, has made that mechanism urgently consequential. When the environment makes structural planes obsolete faster than the developmental trajectory produces readiness to reconstruct them, the question shifts from how effectively a person pursues goals within their meaning framework to whether the framework itself remains viable. Extending the Integrating Structure and Life Energy (ISLE) framework to the individual, the paper treats persons as perceptual entities whose development follows a sequence of S-curves: structural planes consolidating, compressing interpretive elasticity, accumulating misalignment, and approaching coherence horizons. Life energy, the animating construct, operates at a prior level to motivation: where motivation theory presupposes a stable structural plane, life energy determines whether that plane remains viable and whether reconstruction is possible when it does not. Thinking, the premise-generative activity consolidation progressively displaces with execution, is the individual-level variable whose preservation or conversion into execution determines reconstruction. Foundational structural density, established before deliberate examination is possible, shapes thinking capacity before adult consolidation begins. From this mechanism the paper derives a six-orientation typology (architect, striver, floater, seeker, victim, breakdown) as a developmental diagnostic of the person's relationship to life energy and thinking capacity. The integrating variable is reconstruction capacity, which incorporates Fonagy's reflective functioning scale as a validated first component while adding the composite structure RF alone cannot provide. Five testable propositions follow.

detail.abstract:
Objectives: The landscape of AI in healthcare is characterized by a proliferation of guidelines. While many articulate similar principles, they do not always overlap and often lack actionable guidance across the AI lifecycle. This article describes the development of the CHAI Responsible AI Guide and examines how large-scale, multi-stakeholder consensus methods can translate ethical principles into coordinated, adoptable practices across institutional contexts.
Methods: CHAI conducted a yearlong consensus process that combined deliberation across five workgroups, a community-wide survey, multistakeholder review, and independent expert review. The approach drew on modified Delphi methods and is reported using the CREDES framework, with adaptations for participatory design and editorial responsibility analogous to the National Academies.
Results: The process applied five principle-based themes to a six-stage lifecycle framework, generating considerations with representative use cases illustrating how priorities can shift across contexts and stages. Together, these outputs provide a shared vocabulary and practical framework for applying responsible AI principles across development, evaluation, deployment, and monitoring.
Discussion: Unlike prior consensus efforts focused on discrete phases of AI evaluation, this initiative addressed the challenges of coordination, translation, and accountability across the full AI lifecycle. The adaptive consensus design balanced depth of deliberation with broad participation, supporting iterative refinement while incorporating perspectives from a large and diverse stakeholder community.
Conclusion: The CHAI Responsible AI Guide demonstrates how structured, multi-stakeholder collaboration can support lifecycle-based governance for health AI. Its development offers insights for future consensus efforts in complex, rapidly evolving domains where responsibility is distributed across institutions and roles.

title: AI and Financial Risk Governance in Emerging Markets: Regulatory Gaps and Structural Exposure in Latin America

detail.title: AI and Financial Risk Governance in Emerging Markets: Regulatory Gaps and Structural Exposure in Latin America
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence is reshaping credit assessment, fraud detection, payment infrastructure, and systemic risk monitoring across the global financial system. Yet the scholarly literature documenting this transformation is geographically lopsided: bibliometric reviews of AI in financial risk management show research output concentrated in India, China, and the United States, with Latin America occupying a marginal position on the map despite housing some of the fastest-growing instant-payment ecosystems in the world. This monograph addresses that imbalance. It examines how artificial intelligence is being adopted across Latin American banking and financial-supervisory systems, how regulatory frameworks in the region compare to the risk-based approaches emerging in the European Union, the United Kingdom, and the United States, and where structural features specific to the region-high informality, currency volatility, fragmented supervisory capacity, and uneven financial inclusion-create riskmanagement challenges that frameworks built for advanced economies do not fully anticipate. Drawing on regulatory filings, central bank communications, international financial institution reports, and the existing academic literature, the analysis covers comparative regulation, countrylevel adoption patterns in Brazil, Mexico, Chile, and Colombia, algorithmic credit scoring in economies with large informal sectors, and systemic-risk questions raised by AI-intensive payment rails such as Brazil's Pix. The monograph closes with policy recommendations and an explicit research agenda, distinguishing throughout between findings supported by direct regional evidence and propositions that remain, honestly, hypotheses for future empirical work.

title: Algorithm Transparency and Search Manipulation: Steering vs. Persuasion
affiliations: Kelley School of Business, Indiana University,  and University of North Carolina (UNC) at Chapel Hill - Department of Public Policy

detail.title: Algorithm Transparency and Search Manipulation: Steering vs. Persuasion
detail.abstract: We study a platform that prefers to sell the more profitable of two products. It designs an algorithm that determines the product the consumer encounters first, conditional on her best match. The algorithm simultaneously manipulates consumer attention (steers) and communicates information about match quality (informs). When the algorithm is opaque, it is difficult for a consumer to understand how product order is generated and what it reveals. In the platform's preferred equilibrium, it places the profitable product first. When the algorithm is transparent, the consumer understands the algorithm and what it conveys. Thus, the algorithm can persuade as well as steer. In some cases, the equilibrium algorithm deters search, in others, encourages it. In the former case, transparency helps consumers; in the latter, it harms some or all of them. Extending or shifting transparency requirements uncouples steering from information provision, reverting the consumer's welfare to opacity.

title: The AI Productivity Paradox in SMEs Why AI Adoption Does Not Always Translate into Business Performance

detail.title: The AI Productivity Paradox in SMEs Why AI Adoption Does Not Always Translate into Business Performance
detail.abstract: Small and medium enterprises (SMEs) have adopted artificial intelligence tools at a speed that has few precedents among general purpose business technologies, yet the productivity and profitability gains this adoption was expected to deliver remain difficult to detect once the analysis moves from the individual task to the whole firm. This paper examines why AI adoption among SMEs so often fails to translate into measurable business performance, a gap this paper terms the SME AI productivity paradox. Drawing on recent OECD survey data covering more than two thousand SMEs across twelve countries, enterprise-level surveys from McKinsey and the National Bureau of Economic Research, MIT's widely cited GenAI Divide report, and the academic literature on general purpose technologies and organizational resilience, the paper develops a conceptual framework linking four mechanisms to this paradox: missing complementary organizational capital, a task-to-firm value translation gap, resource-constrained fixed costs of complementary investment, and a measurement and cash flow horizon mismatch specific to smaller firms. The analysis finds that these mechanisms compound one another for SMEs in a way they do not for large enterprises, since SMEs typically lack the dedicated staff, training budgets, and multi-year investment horizon that allow larger organizations to work through the early, unproductive phase of a general purpose technology's diffusion. The paper illustrates this compounding effect with evidence from Pakistan, where infrastructure and financing constraints add a further layer to the skills and organizational-capital barriers documented in advanced-economy survey data. The paper closes with a practical, resource-conscious framework SMEs can use to sequence AI investment, and with implications for policy design aimed at closing the adoption-to-performance gap.

detail.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) engines are increasingly used for business and financial work, including tasks that resemble the calculations performed by investment banks and private equity firms. We evaluated the capability of three frontier LLMs to solve open-ended leveraged buyout (LBO) modeling problems. We utilized Python and Excel to generate 100 synthetic cases across three tiers of difficulty, and we fed each case separately as a fresh conversation to each LLM. We prompted each LLM to generate eleven LBO-related parameters with a formula-driven ground truth that was independently reconciled between Excel and Python. ChatGPT correctly solved 63 of the 100 LBO cases (63%); Claude correctly solved 58 of the 100 LBO cases (58%); Gemini correctly solved 42 of the 100 LBO cases (42%). We observed that LLM accuracy declined as the LBO case structure complexity increased. The models were generally reliable when calculating purchase enterprise value, initial debt, sponsor equity, EBITDA, and exit enterprise value, but they were substantially less reliable when linking debt repayment to exit equity, investor internal rate of return, and money-on-money multiple. These findings indicate that contemporary LLM engines can sometimes adequately perform isolated LBO calculations, but none should be relied upon without deterministic verification and professional review for a complete LBO transaction model.

title: Cyclical Reproduction: A Process Ontology of Complex Systems

detail.title: Cyclical Reproduction: A Process Ontology of Complex Systems
detail.abstract: This paper articulates and defends a process-ontological account according to which the most complex systems exist through cyclical reproduction rather than through material persistence. The conventional view treats existence as material continuity: a system exists because its constituents persist, and terminates when they fail. This is correct for simple physical systems but inadequate for systems of greater complexity, where constituents are continuously replaced and apparent stability is the product of cyclical processes. The paper articulates the foundational claim, draws the simple/complex distinction precisely, and develops the architecture into four nested kingdoms: cosmological, planetary, biological, and civilisational. Each kingdom is constituted by cycles its constituents do not contain, and the relations between them are articulated through three principles of cyclical dynamics: upward constraint, upward emergence, and downward causation. Reflexive agency is identified as the addition that constitutes the civilisational kingdom: the capacity of agents to form representations of the systems they participate in and act on those representations in ways that modify the systems. The paper engages the principal antecedents in Whitehead's process philosophy, Maturana and Varela's autopoietic theory, and Luhmann's autopoietic social systems, and the principal challenges from Kim's exclusion argument, from the charge of teleological smuggling, and from the objection that the four kingdoms are folk taxonomy. It closes by stating what the framework commits to and what it does not.

title: Innovationology and the Geoeconomic Rise of BRICS: Toward a Plural Techno-Economic Order
affiliations: African Research Network (ARN)

detail.title: Innovationology and the Geoeconomic Rise of BRICS: Toward a Plural Techno-Economic Order
detail.abstract: The rise of Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa (BRICS) is reshaping the geography of global economic and technological power. This article develops Innovationology as a transdisciplinary framework for examining how societies generate, adapt, and strategically deploy innovation across technological, institutional, productive, and geopolitical domains. Through comparative analysis of the five original BRICS economies, it examines research and development, technological capabilities, digital transformation, entrepreneurship, industrial upgrading, and technological autonomy. The findings reveal substantial heterogeneity rather than a unified BRICS innovation model. Brazil demonstrates strengths in agritech, bioeconomy, energy, and digital finance; Russia in strategic science and statecoordinated technologies; India in digital infrastructure, entrepreneurship, and scalable innovation; China in large-scale research, manufacturing, and technological upgrading; and South Africa in scientific and resource-linked innovation. The article argues that BRICS is not creating a homogeneous alternative to the Western innovation system. Rather, its significance lies in the aggregation of diverse and partially complementary capabilities that contribute to a more plural and polycentric global techno-economic order. Innovationology offers a framework for understanding how these capabilities translate into productive transformation, technological autonomy, and geoeconomic influence.

title:
Branding Coexists With Market: Every Ad Is a Brand Deposit
Building Long-Term Trust Among Small Service Enterprises in Durban: A Qualitative Field Analysis

detail.title:
Branding Coexists With Market: Every Ad Is a Brand Deposit
Building Long-Term Trust Among Small Service Enterprises in Durban: A Qualitative Field Analysis
detail.abstract: This working paper introduces the Brand Deposit Framework, a strategic model designed to evaluate the long-term brand equity impacts of daily marketing activities among small and medium service enterprises (SMEs) in Durban, South Africa. Operating within resourceconstrained emerging markets, small business founders face a critical tension between immediate revenue generation and sustainable reputation. Utilizing a qualitative observational field methodology, this study analyzes the marketing and advertising behaviors of 24 small businesses across three primary consumer sectors in the Durban metropolitan area: independent skincare brands (n=6), automotive dealerships (n=12), and health and wellness centers (n=6). The paper categorizes promotional strategies into two distinct operational paradigms: Brand Deposits-defined as educational, empathetic, and dignity-preserving communications-and Brand Withdrawals-characterized by fear-based, deceptive, or hidden-cost tactics designed to induce immediate transactions. The field observations indicate that while 'withdrawal' marketing generates short-term transaction spikes, it ultimately degrades consumer trust, increases customer churn, and erodes the collective reputation of local small businesses. Conversely, 'deposit' marketing fosters longterm pricing power and customer retention. The study concludes with an actionable "Deposit vs. Withdrawal Audit" tool, allowing emerging market entrepreneurs to systematically align shortterm promotional tactics with long-term reputational capital.

detail.abstract:
This article examines the 114-kilometre freeway corridor linking Alkimos, in Perth's northern suburbs, to Mandurah, in the south. The corridor carries one of Western Australia's densest concentrations of automated speed, average-speed and AI-assisted mobile-phone and seatbelt detection cameras. The cameras are officially described as a safety measure. 

This article suggests, instead, that the corridor's camera network functions in substance as an indirect tax on a constrained, high-income, time-poor population: the blue-collar Fly-In Fly-Out (FIFO) workforce of Western Australia's mining industry, for whom the corridor is the principal route to Perth Airport. It draws on the economic model of compliance developed by Allingham and Sandmo and on Valerie Braithwaite's typology of motivational postures to explain why this cohort settles infringements passively rather than contesting them. It examines Regulation 265 of the Road Traffic Code 2000 (WA) as an example of drafting apparently suited to automated capture rather than to the ordinary meaning of driver distraction and considers the Road Traffic Legislation Amendment (Infringement Management Reform) Act 2024 (WA), longitudinal fatality data, and the spatial distribution of camera infrastructure as evidence against the official safety narrative. It concludes with recommendations directed at realigning enforcement with demonstrated risk.

title: Photonic Quantum Computing vs. Classical Solvers in Constrained Factor Portfolio Optimization
affiliations: , Singapore Management University - Lee Kong Chian School of Business and School of Computing and Information Systems, Singapore Management University

detail.title: Photonic Quantum Computing vs. Classical Solvers in Constrained Factor Portfolio Optimization
detail.abstract:
The authors present a rigorous empirical evaluation of three distinct optimization paradigms for institutional
factor portfolio construction: an entropy-based photonic quantum annealer (Dirac-3, Quantum Computing
Inc.), a commercial mixed-integer programming solver (Gurobi), and a model-free deep reinforcement
learning agent (SAC). Evaluating these pipelines on the Jensen–Kelly–Pedersen 13-factor equity library
across 164 months test window, we implement a full factorial penalty sweep comprising 48 hyperparameter
configurations that govern return, volatility, and skewness trade-offs. Our findings demonstrate that while
photonic hardware can locate superior risk-return topologies within a narrow operating range, classical
mixed-integer programming remains superior for risk-constrained mandates requiring tight tail-risk control
and cross-seed stability. Furthermore, we document structural failure modes in reinforcement learning factor
allocators under unanchored higher-moment shaping. We translate these empirical results into actionable,
mandate-specific guidelines for quantitative portfolio managers deploying advanced optimization engines.

title: Can GDELT News Sentiment Predict Macro Equity and Bond Futures?
affiliations: University of Virginia

detail.title: Can GDELT News Sentiment Predict Macro Equity and Bond Futures?
detail.abstract: This paper explores whether news sentiment and volume data from the Global Database of Events, Language, and Tone (GDELT) can generate trading signals for global equity and bond futures. We aggregate GDELT tone and volume to the country-subnarrative-day grain across 14 economic, political, and social themes. We then evaluate three trading frameworks on the same features. The first is an event-driven strategy that triggers on extreme rolling z-scores of polarity or positive-or negative-volume change. The other two are cross-sectional panel models. One is an OLS regression on standardized sentiment features. The other is a logistic regression on the sign of forward returns. The panel models are run in a daily-aligned regime and a weekly-aligned regime. The sample covers 22 equity and 9 bond futures across the Americas, Europe, and Asia-Pacific from 2015 to 2026. In the per-region event study, only 3 of 974 configurations exceed a Sharpe of 1.0 and 52 exceed 0.5, which suggests the top entries may be spurious given the size of the search. The best per-region Sharpes are 2.32 for equity futures and 1.38 for bond futures, with Labor Productivity, Fiscal Policy, and Employment appearing frequently at the top. The pooled global event study is weaker at the top, with a best Sharpe of 0.93, and none of the 372 pooled configurations exceeding 1.0. Both panel models are weak in both aligned regimes: No configuration reaches an outof-sample Sharpe of 0.5 in any of the four (model, horizon, rebalance) cells with median Sharpe being negative in every cell. The best aligned-regime panel Sharpe we obtain is 0.26. Taken together, the results are suggest that GDELT sentiment carries limited cross-sectional predictive power for macro futures.

title: Recursive Bayesian Compression and False Certainty

detail.title: Recursive Bayesian Compression and False Certainty
detail.abstract: A fully Bayesian learner retains everything that past observations imply about an uncertain state. We study a learner who instead keeps only separate assessments of two components of the state: after each new signal, she updates correctly, records the two posterior marginals, discards their association, and before the next signal reconstructs a joint belief by treating those marginals as independent. Thus every signal is observed and the statistical model is correct, but information created by earlier updating can be lost between periods. We characterize when this repeated compression can lead the learner to become certain of a false state. A state can attract learning when it explains the data better than every alternative obtained by changing only one of its components, even though another state provides a better overall explanation. In a binary environment, we show that this mechanism is robust: throughout an open set of correctly specified models, the compressed learner converges to certainty in a particular false state with positive probability. Finally, we characterize when marginal records lose no information relevant for future learning: this happens exactly when each signal affects the two state components in a multiplicatively separable way, so that Bayesian updating never creates association between them. With two binary components, storing one additional measure of association is enough to restore exact Bayesian updating.

detail.abstract: This study examines the constitutional specificities of access to justice for climate change issues. title: An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of the People, II: The Political Economy of Inflation - A Dynamic Monetary Formula, Responsibility Attribution, and the Limits of Monetary Redistribution
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of the People, II: The Political Economy of Inflation - A Dynamic Monetary Formula, Responsibility Attribution, and the Limits of Monetary Redistribution
detail.abstract: This paper proposes a dynamic monetary formula that analytically separates inflation into a reasonable component and an excess component, and argues, from a political-economic perspective, for the attribution of responsibility for the excess component. Unlike traditional monetarism and the Austrian School, the paper both acknowledges the necessity of mild inflation and uses formal methods to draw the boundary between what is "reasonable" and what constitutes "invisible taxation." The single free parameter of the resulting benchmark is not endogenized; instead, two rules govern how it is taken in accounting, so that numerical conclusions never depend on its specific value. By deconstructing the three-layer composition of the monetary increment ∆M , the paper exposes the rent-seeking structure behind excess inflation and the mechanism of wealth transfer that accompanies it. A parallelogram model of wealth distribution is introduced to argue that, when a transfer is financed by money creation and the excess growth is not absorbed by a decline in velocity, "an increase in the monetary figures held by lower-income populations" and "inflation" are two observational perspectives on one and the same event. The paper locates the real short-run stabilization gains of monetary expansion inside the same framework, as the phase in which the absorption channel is open, and shows that under quantitative constraints monetary expansion cannot durably deliver trend improvement in the real wealth of lower-income populations.

title: A Corporate Framework for Evidence Mapping to the IUCN Global Standard for Nature-Based Solutions

detail.title: A Corporate Framework for Evidence Mapping to the IUCN Global Standard for Nature-Based Solutions
detail.abstract: Nature-based Solutions (NbS) are gaining traction in corporate sustainability strategies, yet organizations often struggle to translate dispersed documentation into verification-ready assessments aligned with the IUCN Global Standard and its Self-Assessment Tool (SAT). This paper introduces a structured, evidence-based approach that enables companies to map existing artefacts, such as policies, monitoring reports, and budgets, against the Standard's eight criteria and 28 indicators, ensuring transparency and traceability without requiring bespoke data collection. The methodology emphasizes systematic evidence organization, indicator-level analysis, and qualitative synthesis to produce credible, audit-friendly outputs for disclosure frameworks like TNFD and SBTN. Demonstrated through a corporate NbS case study, the approach highlights how structured documentation and iterative gap closure can strengthen integrity and readiness for independent verification. By bridging the gap between planning artefacts and compliance requirements, this framework supports businesses in accelerating nature-positive transitions, enhancing ESG reporting, meeting global biodiversity and climate goals, and strengthening confidence in nature-related disclosures among investors, regulators, and other stakeholders.

title: The Legal Regime of Shipwrecks with Emphasis on Environmental Law
affiliations: NATIONAL KAPODISTRIAN UNIVERSITY OF ATHENS

detail.title: The Legal Regime of Shipwrecks with Emphasis on Environmental Law
detail.abstract: Shipwrecks occupy an unstable legal position. They may be navigational hazards, sources of oil or chemical pollution, objects of salvage, abandoned property, evidence of maritime casualties, gravesites, or underwater cultural heritage. Environmental law does not abolish these classifications, but it changes their hierarchy. A wreck which threatens the marine environment cannot be treated merely as an object of private maritime law. It becomes a locus of public duties: prevention, precaution, cooperation, notification, response, removal, restoration, and compensation. The central legal development is the Nairobi International Convention on the Removal of Wrecks, 2007, which gives affected coastal States a structured power to require removal of hazardous wrecks and to recover costs from the registered owner, supported by compulsory insurance. The Convention, however, is only one part of a wider legal field. UNCLOS supplies the constitutional frame for marine environmental protection; MARPOL addresses pollution from ships from operational and accidental causes; OPRC and OPRC-HNS organize preparedness and response; the CLC, Fund and Bunkers regimes allocate liability for oil pollution; EU law adds waste, environmental liability, criminal and operational response dimensions; and the UNESCO 2001 Convention protects wrecks that have acquired cultural character. The result is a layered regime in which the classification of a wreck depends less on its historical or proprietary identity than on risk, jurisdictional location, environmental harm, and the capacity of the coastal State to intervene lawfully and proportionately.

title: Heterogeneous Attention and Macroeconomic Dynamics:Theory and LLM Experiments

detail.title: Heterogeneous Attention and Macroeconomic Dynamics:Theory and LLM Experiments
detail.abstract: We develop a rational inattention model in which agents differ in cognitive processing capacity. Heterogeneous cognitive discounting generates horizon-dependent policy attenuation, cross-sectional MPC dispersion, and a sufficient statistic—the squared coefficient of variation of attention—that captures the aggregate cost of ignoring heterogeneity and grows quadratically with the policy horizon. The same mechanism microfounds the excess sensitivity parameter and partially resolves the excess smoothness puzzle. Since cognitive capacity is latent and confounded with preferences in human data, we deploy six LLMs of varying scale as computational households—exploiting exogenous, architecture-determined variation in processing capacity. The experiments confirm the predicted capacity–smoothing gradient: frontier models track the perfectforesight benchmark while smaller models are an order of magnitude more volatile, though the ranking is not monotone in parameter count.

title: Environmental Permitting and Environmental Impact Assessment in the United States and the European Union: A Comparative Legal Study
affiliations: NATIONAL KAPODISTRIAN UNIVERSITY OF ATHENS

detail.title: Environmental Permitting and Environmental Impact Assessment in the United States and the European Union: A Comparative Legal Study
detail.abstract: Environmental permitting is one of the principal legal techniques through which contemporary legal systems translate environmental protection from a general public objective into a condition governing concrete projects. Yet the United States and the European Union organize this function through markedly different institutional and doctrinal structures. In the United States, the National Environmental Policy Act operates primarily as a procedural framework for federal decision-making and is superimposed upon sector-specific permitting regimes under statutes such as the Clean Water Act and the Clean Air Act. In the European Union, environmental assessment is embedded within a denser supranational framework in which the Environmental Impact Assessment Directive establishes binding requirements for the authorization of public and private projects, while parallel instruments concerning habitats, water, industrial emissions and public participation may impose additional substantive constraints. This study compares the scope, screening mechanisms, assessment requirements, treatment of alternatives, public participation, judicial review and substantive legal effects of the two systems. Particular attention is paid to the recent evolution of United States law, including Seven County Infrastructure Coalition v Eagle County, and to the jurisprudence of the Court of Justice of the European Union. The comparison demonstrates that the two systems share a common preventive logic but diverge significantly as to the legal intensity of environmental assessment and its relationship with the final authorization decision.

title: Agroforestry as a Livelihood Transition in Post-Illegal-Mining Landscapes: A Scenario-Based Financial Appraisal for Indonesia
affiliations: and

detail.title: Agroforestry as a Livelihood Transition in Post-Illegal-Mining Landscapes: A Scenario-Based Financial Appraisal for Indonesia
detail.abstract: Illegal and poorly regulated mining can leave forest landscapes with severe soil degradation, disrupted hydrology, uncertain tenure, and communities whose short-term income remains tied to extraction. Agroforestry is frequently proposed as a restorative livelihood strategy, yet claims about its economic feasibility are often made without transparent cash-flow assumptions or sensitivity tests. This paper combines a structured narrative synthesis of peerreviewed and official sources with an illustrative 10-year, per-hectare discounted cash-flow scenario for Indonesia. The appraisal uses constant Indonesian rupiah, a 10% discount rate, and four indicators: net present value (NPV), benefit-cost ratio (BCR), internal rate of return (IRR), and payback period. The evidence synthesis shows that agroforestry can link land rehabilitation with staged income from annual crops, non-timber forest products, perennial crops, and timber, but only when site safety, tenure, finance, market access, and local organization are addressed. Under the base scenario, the model produces an NPV of IDR 50.91 million per hectare, a BCR of 2.35, an IRR of 74.30%, and an undiscounted payback period of 2.88 years. A joint 10% reduction in benefits and 10% increase in costs lowers the NPV to IDR 38.27 million, the BCR to 1.92, and the IRR to 54.11%. Delaying all benefits by one year yields an NPV of IDR 35.84 million, a BCR of 1.95, an IRR of 40.77%, and a payback period of 4.27 years. These results describe an optimistic planning scenario rather than observed project performance. The main contribution is therefore not a universal profitability claim, but a transparent appraisal and implementation framework that can be replaced with site-specific field, price, labor, and ecological data before investment or policy decisions are made.

detail.abstract: This study examines the geography of healthcare inequality for women and children across West Bengal. A women and child healthcare index (WCHI) has been constructed for 2015 and 2019 using a two-stage Principal Component Analysis (PCA) based on twenty indicators distilled into three dimensions. The results reveal considerable variation in healthcare outcomes across districts. Among the different dimensions, teenage pregnancy and child nutrition emerge as the most critical areas requiring policy attention. Spatial analysis using Moran's I and Local Indicators of Spatial Association (LISA) cluster maps indicates that district-level health outcomes exhibit increasing spatial dependence, particularly in 2019, suggesting that the healthcare conditions of neighbouring districts are closely linked. Further, the spatial lag model identifies population pressure on doctors and hospital beds have significant influencing healthcare outcomes across space. These findings highlight the policies to strengthening public healthcare infrastructure and other institutional factors to improve women's and children's health across West Bengal.

title: Rationing, Arbitrage and Expectations: A Structural Model of Zimbabwe's Parallel Foreign Exchange Premium

detail.title: Rationing, Arbitrage and Expectations: A Structural Model of Zimbabwe's Parallel Foreign Exchange Premium
detail.abstract: Zimbabwe's foreign exchange market has, for most of the period since 2019, exhibited a persistent and economically damaging gap between the official bank-quoted USD rate and the informal ("street") rate. This paper develops a three-layer structural model of that gap. First, an individual's currency-sourcing decision is shown to be a linear programme whose Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions imply a corner solution-agents exhaust cheap, quota-rationed bank access before turning to the parallel market-which explains why quota systems are prone to leakage and resale rather than reaching end users. Second, a static supply-demand model shows the premium is the shadow price of a binding official-rate price ceiling, formalising the standard rationing account. Third, a no-arbitrage condition determines the minimum margin required to compensate informal dealers for enforcement risk and search costs, decomposing the observed premium into a scarcity component and a risk-compensation component. Fourth, and most novel, a stock-flow model with one-period-lagged, premium-based expectations is reduced to a firstorder linear difference equation in the premium; a stability theorem is proved showing convergence to a finite steady-state premium if and only if speculative demand's sensitivity to the lagged premium is smaller than informal supply's sensitivity to the current premium-and that, consistent with Dornbusch (1986) and Pinto (1986), the steady-state premium depends on the rate of money creation rather than the level of the official exchange rate. The model's qualitative predictions are checked against Zimbabwe's 2019-2026 experience, including the ZiG currency reform, the September 2024 devaluation, and the premium's narrowing from over 100 percent to approximately 20 percent by early 2026.

title: Institutional Delay as Governance Failure

detail.title: Institutional Delay as Governance Failure
detail.abstract:
Institutional delay is not administrative friction. It is a governance act. When a public body or regulated institution runs a repeatable delay pattern against an identified individual-cycling correspondence through insufficiency demands, circular referrals, precondition stacking, template dismissals, identity gates, or channel redirects-that pattern constitutes a decision not to decide. Under existing accountability frameworks, including the Nolan Principles and the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, such non-decisions carry the same obligations as affirmative ones: a named human being must be accountable for them.
This paper introduces a formal taxonomy of six institutional delay patterns derived from documented correspondence across UK local government, financial services, regulatory bodies, and standards commissions. Each pattern is identified, classified, and evidenced from live casework conducted under the Burgess Principle (UK Certification Mark UK00004343685), a registered binary accountability standard that classifies institutional decisions as SOVEREIGN (a named human applied their mind to the specific facts of an identified individual’s case) or NULL (no such application is evidenced).
The paper presents a dual-signal classification architecture that deliberately separates two questions that existing governance tools conflate: (1) is a delay pattern present in the correspondence? and (2) was a named human accountable for the decision that produced it? By maintaining this separation, the framework avoids both over-claiming — treating pattern detection as a legal finding — and under-delivering — presenting raw evidence without classification.
The taxonomy is presented in a restorative register consistent with the series thesis stated in The SOVEREIGN Decline (2026f): the framework exists not to catalogue individual failure but to identify where institutional design has dissolved attributable judgment into process, and to specify — at the minimum cost available — the conditions under which it is returned to a named person. Each delay pattern is paired with its SOVEREIGN exit: the documented, achievable output that closes the loop and returns standing to both the individual and the institution.
A machine-readable schema (loop-finding.v1.json) and an advisory classification endpoint (/loop/classify) are published as part of the open-source Burgess Principle stack. The endpoint enforces a mandatory human confirmation gate before any finding can be exported to the public certification register. The tool practises what the standard preaches.

title: Racialized Red Tape: Unraveling Administrative Burdens in Liquor Licensing
affiliations: University of Oregon - School of Law

detail.title: Racialized Red Tape: Unraveling Administrative Burdens in Liquor Licensing
detail.abstract: Americans often bemoan 'red tape' as cumbersome but necessary formalities within administrative governance. Though frustrating, red tape seems to assuage public confidence by portraying bureaucratic decisionmaking as democratic, thorough, and-most importantlyimpartial. This Article counters that passive frame, repositioning administrative procedures as active producers of structural inequity. Drawing on the experiences of small minority-owned businesses seeking to obtain or retain liquor licenses, this Article constructs regulatory bodies as sites that delineate access, agency, and belonging among marginalized groups despite decades of equity interventions. Part I contextualizes liquor licensing within this endeavor, situating it as an unassuming administrative practice that underlies historical and contemporary disparities in spatial and economic autonomy. Part II evaluates the role of state agencies and agents in advancing "racialized administrative burdens," or the learning, psychological, and compliance barriers that conceal exclusionary practices. Relying on qualitative focused case narratives, Part III interprets how racialized administrative burdens in liquor licensing are both operationalized and insulated through normative appeals to neutrality and public safety. Part IV prescribes “historically informed rulemaking” as an analytical framework for rule design and enforcement in contested regulatory domains. This Article invites legal scholars, policymakers, and agency officials to take seriously the distributive properties of bureaucratic procedure.

detail.abstract: Education for Sustainable Development (ESD) has become an important component of global efforts to achieve the Sustainable Development Goals, with governments playing a central role in its integration into national education and sustainable development policies. However, limited research has examined how different forms of government influence ESD implementation, particularly in the diverse political context of Southeast Asia. This literature review examines the relationship between government type and ESD implementation in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) by synthesizing literature on governance, climate change, sustainable development, and education, alongside country-level ESD policies and strategies. The review finds that ASEAN countries demonstrate diverse approaches to ESD across different government types, with no clear or consistent relationship between regime type and the presence or implementation of ESD policies. Factors such as political stability, economic conditions, governance capacity, international assistance, and stakeholder participation appear to interact with government structures in shaping ESD outcomes. The review therefore suggests that government type alone is insufficient to explain differences in ESD implementation across ASEAN. Further quantitative and qualitative research is needed to examine the specific institutional and contextual factors that enable or constrain ESD integration in the region.

title: Cash Conversion Cycle Management, Pro tability, and Crisis Resilience: Evidence from Brazilian Private Firms (2009 2024)
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, and Getulio Vargas Foundation (FGV) - Sao Paulo School of Economics

detail.title: Cash Conversion Cycle Management, Pro tability, and Crisis Resilience: Evidence from Brazilian Private Firms (2009 2024)
detail.abstract: We examine how the cash conversion cycle (CCC) relates to rm pro tability and nancial resilience across normal and crisis periods, using a balanced panel of 87 Brazilian privately held rms over 2009 2024. Extending prior work on working capital management in emerging markets, we exploit the COVID-19 pandemic as an exogenous shock to decompose the mechanisms through which crises disrupt CCC components. Estimating dynamic panel regressions via generalized method of moments (GMM) and a di erence-in-di erences (DID) design, we con rm that shorter CCC improves return on assets (ROA) but not return on equity (ROE). Crucially, we document a sharp and asymmetric disruption in the payment cycle during 2020: days payable outstanding collapsed from a pre-crisis average of 24,149 to 1,604 a reduction of over 93% while days sales outstanding and days inventory outstanding remained broadly stable. This nding reveals that supplier-side trade credit contraction was the primary working capital mechanism of COVID-19 for private Brazilian rms. Using a quadrant framework based on rms’ equity and receivables pro les, we show that the shock was concentrated among low-equity/high-receivables rms (DID ≈ 47,000, p < 0.05), while high-equity/low-receivables rms were entirely insulated. The CCC values reported throughout this paper are measured in the natural unit of the ValorPRO database (see Section 3 for a detailed discussion of scale and plausibility).

detail.abstract: Cramér's V, the effect size reported beside almost every chi-square test, is almost never accompanied by a confidence interval, because the interval is a hard nuisance-parameter problem: infinitely many tables share one effect-size value. The two intervals an analyst can reach for are unsatisfactory. The projection of a joint confidence region onto the effect size is guaranteed for every table but wide, over-covering at essentially 1.000 on larger tables; the noncentral inversion the software prints, and the bootstrap, are narrow but do not cover (median coverage 0.31 on this study's grid). This paper supplies an interval that is both valid and informative. Conditioning on the observed margins makes the exact conditional distribution of the Pearson statistic under a non-null association computable with no asymptotics and no Monte Carlo; inverting it yields a near-nominal confidence interval for Cramér's V that is a third to a half the width of the projection, the advantage growing with table size. The one price, stated plainly, is a change of estimand to the effect size at the observed margins; the mid-p default undercovers small effects, where a conservative variant or the projection remains the fallback.

title: The Priced Dimensions of Asymmetric Risk

detail.title: The Priced Dimensions of Asymmetric Risk
detail.abstract: Do the many measures of asymmetric risk identify one downside factor or several priced dimensions? We study compensation for asymmetric risk in U.S. equities, separating robust premia, distinct return variation, and priced dimensions. Five measure families organize around three recurring priced dimensions rather than a single downside factor. Multiple dimensions receive compensation across periods and portfolio constructions, although their relative pricing strength varies over time. The resulting three-factor benchmark is not jointly spanned by leading factor models. The dimensions also exhibit distinct predictive relations with aggregate conditions. The results distinguish new measures from new priced risks.

title: The Uniform-Target Dilemma in Industrial Policy
affiliations: Renmin University of China - School of Finance and Renmin University of China - School of Finance

detail.title: The Uniform-Target Dilemma in Industrial Policy
detail.abstract: Industrial policy faces a uniform-target dilemma: a common target can coordinate upgrading for firms already close to it, yet encourage observable compliance rather than substantive investment among firms farther away. Using 2.85 million Chinese firm-years, we construct policy leap distance, the product-space distance between firms' existing products and municipal policy targets. Policy leap distance is negatively related to firm productivity, and this relationship is nonlinear: moderate distance is associated with higher productivity, but the effect turns negative as targets move beyond a moderate distance and intensifies sharply for the most distant targets. Because a majority of firm-years face targets beyond this turning point, the distortion affects most firms rather than a small tail. The distortion is organizational on both sides: firms raise reportable R&D and entertainment spending while patenting less, and municipal governments write vaguer, more proceduredependent policies. These distant targets are not a response to local conditions: they are transmitted top-down as provincial and central policy narratives diffuse, largely independent of local officials' characteristics. External oversight partially corrects the distortion: central inspection shocks reduce municipal policy distance and dampen the firm-side response to distant targets.

title: The Control Perimeter - AI Control, the Deployment Protocol, and the Institution No Evaluation Reaches

detail.title: The Control Perimeter - AI Control, the Deployment Protocol, and the Institution No Evaluation Reaches
detail.abstract: The AI control agenda accepts a premise most of alignment research resists: that safety may have to be secured without trusting the model. Rather than trying to make a system want the right things, control asks how to prevent a system that wants the wrong things from causing unacceptable harm, and answers with deployment protocols, monitoring, auditing, restricted affordances, trusted substitution, whose adequacy is estimated by a red-team procedure the agenda calls a control evaluation. This paper takes the agenda seriously and on its own terms. Its claim is not that control is mistaken. Its claim is that control has a boundary it has not drawn. A control evaluation is defined over a model, a protocol, and a fixed deployment context, all inside the developer's environment. It certifies a safety property of that arrangement. It does not evaluate the institution that adopts the model, becomes dependent on it, and thereby acquires the capacity to cause the very harms the protocol was meant to bound. I call the boundary within which a protocol's guarantee holds the control perimeter, and I argue that the perimeter stops at the developer's sandbox while the power the evaluation is meant to govern has already moved outside it. The paper reconstructs the agenda's core instruments and transposes each from the model to the deploying institution, showing that the transposed problem is real, unaddressed, and in most cases invisible to the methods control has built. It closes with the minimal design a control evaluation would need in order to reach the deployer: a monitored decision surface, a demonstrated fallback, an externally triggerable audit channel, and an assigned controller for the institution rather than the model. The argument is offered as an extension of the control program, not a rejection of it.

title: Bias Against Mobile Capital: Evidence from U.S. Environmental Enforcement

detail.title: Bias Against Mobile Capital: Evidence from U.S. Environmental Enforcement
detail.abstract: Do governments discriminate against foreign-owned firms in enforcing regulations? Politicians may favor domestic-owned firms through relaxed enforcement. Yet foreign-owned firms can face discrimination even under politicians who are not protectionist and value stringent regulation: an information-driven bias by bureaucratic regulators. Pro-regulatory politicians task bureaucrats with enforcement, which requires detecting violations that are not perfectly observable. External ownership---foreign or domestic non-local---may signal less familiarity with local regulations and greater violation risk, especially where politicians have promoted stringent rules. Regulators therefore target externally owned firms for additional scrutiny, such as inspections. I examine U.S. environmental regulation, where states can adopt stricter standards and conduct most enforcement. I link administrative records of scrutiny and penalties to ownership data covering 2.4 million plants since 1989. Scrutiny rises after plants are taken over by foreign owners while remaining unchanged after in-state takeovers. This reaction reflects information-driven discrimination rather than protectionism. It extends to domestic out-of-state takeovers. It is concentrated in Democratic strongholds, where pro-regulatory politicians have promoted stringent state-specific regulations. Penalty decisions show no comparable ownership bias but favor campaign donors. Information-driven bias within the bureaucracy, not protectionism, drives discrimination against foreign investors.

title: Engagement Without Endorsement: The Limits of Influencer Prosocial Behavior
affiliations: Boston College - Department of Marketing, University of British Columbia (UBC) - Sauder School of Business and Toronto Metropolitan University

detail.title: Engagement Without Endorsement: The Limits of Influencer Prosocial Behavior
detail.abstract: Influencers increasingly post about their prosocial acts, including monetary donations, in-kind support, and symbolic gestures. Whether such displays of virtue are rewarded, and how they shape audience engagement, remain unclear. Using a large-scale dataset from a major Chinese social media platform, the authors find that prosocial posts increase likes per view but decrease shares per view, with the share penalty concentrated among highly commercial influencers. Likes and shares occupy distinct points on an engagement spectrum: likes convey light-touch approval, whereas shares redistribute the content into audiences' own networks under their name. Prosocial posts may therefore generate engagement without endorsement. The authors complement the field study with a controlled experiment. By randomly varying an influencer's commercial track record, the experiment shows how commercialization can prevent prosocial content from translating into endorsement and identifies reduced source credibility as the underlying mechanism. Because likes vastly outnumber shares, aggregate engagement can make such posts appear successful while masking an erosion of endorsement. Together, these findings reveal a limit to virtue as a reputational corrective: doing good does not undo the reputational cost of doing well commercially.

title: Building High-Performance Educational Organisations Through Effective Leadership
affiliations: Oxford Academy and George Mason University

detail.title: Building High-Performance Educational Organisations Through Effective Leadership
detail.abstract:
Educational organisations are expected to deliver learning quality, equity, resilience, and continuous improvement under resource pressure and social change. Leadership is frequently presented as the mechanism that converts policy and resources into organisational performance, yet the relationship is indirect and context-sensitive. This thesis examines how effective leadership can contribute to high-performance educational organisations, using Jordan as the primary setting, the United Kingdom as an international comparator, and selected Middle Eastern systems as regional benchmarks. A pragmatic comparative case-study design integrates published OECD Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) 2022 indicators, official policy documents, and a structured synthesis of leadership literature. The evidence covers 7,799 students in 260 schools in Jordan and 12,972 students in 451 schools in the United Kingdom. Descriptive analysis compares achievement, minimum proficiency, school autonomy, staffing constraints, resources, and continuity-of-learning indicators. It does not attribute national score differences causally to leadership.

Jordan shows a substantial performance and proficiency gap relative to the United Kingdom, accompanied by large differences in selected school decision rights. Only 5% of students in Jordan attended schools where principals had the main responsibility for hiring teachers and 3% attended schools where teachers had the main responsibility for choosing learning materials; corresponding United Kingdom figures were 81% and 89%. Staffing shortages affected both systems, but exposure to inadequate or poorly qualified staff was markedly higher in Jordan. The findings indicate that high performance cannot be reduced to one leadership style or to autonomy alone. It requires an aligned architecture combining strategic direction, instructional leadership, professional capability, distributed participation, bounded autonomy, reciprocal accountability, evidence-informed improvement, and resilience. The thesis proposes a six-domain High-Performance Educational Leadership and Organisation framework and a phased implementation roadmap. Its principal contribution is a context-sensitive model that treats leadership as an organisational capability rather than a heroic individual trait.

title: Powering Intelligence - A 50-State Analysis of Electricity Economics, Tax Incentives and Regulatory Risk for AI Data Center Investment

detail.title: Powering Intelligence - A 50-State Analysis of Electricity Economics, Tax Incentives and Regulatory Risk for AI Data Center Investment
detail.abstract:
Electricity has quietly become the single largest constraint on the build-out of artificial intelligence infrastructure in the United States. Industry load-growth forecasts now point to data centers consuming a high-single-digit share of total U.S. electricity by the end of the decade, up from roughly 4% only a few years ago [1], and the effect is already visible in the generation mix: coal-fired generation, which had been in structural decline for over a decade, rose approximately 13% in 2025 as grid operators delayed retirements under emergency federal orders to keep pace with demand [2]. For an industry that has spent three years fixated on GPU allocation, the binding constraint has shifted decisively to power — interconnection queues, transmission capacity, and the price of a kilowatt-hour now weigh as heavily on site-selection decisions as chip supply.

This report does three things a conventional cost comparison does not. First, it benchmarks electricity cost and generation mix across all 50 states and the District of Columbia using U.S. Energy Information Administration (“EIA”) data. Second, it introduces the AI Power Competitiveness Index (“PCI”), a weighted, reproducible scoring model that combines electricity cost, state tax competitiveness, incentive generosity, and — critically — regulatory and litigation risk, since the cheapest state on paper is not necessarily the most investable state in practice. Third, it tracks the fast-moving legal and regulatory record as of 11 August 2026, because the incentive and rate landscape for large loads has changed more in the last twelve months than in the prior decade combined.

On a purely economic basis — electricity price, tax competitiveness, incentive depth, and regulatory stability weighted together — our model ranks Texas, New Mexico, Tennessee, Iowa, and Wyoming as the five most competitive states for new AI data-center capacity in 2026 (Section 4). Notably, Virginia — home to the world's largest concentration of data centers — and Illinois fall toward the bottom of the risk-adjusted ranking despite (or in Virginia's case, partly because of) their scale, illustrating that first-mover advantage and incumbent infrastructure are not the same thing as forward risk-adjusted competitiveness.

This is a fast-moving fact pattern. Governor Abbott ordered Texas regulators to pause approval of all new data-center grid connections pending an audit as recently as 3 August 2026 [7] — eight days before this report's issue date — while the Louisiana Public Service Commission was still resolving discovery disputes over a $21 billion Entergy/Meta generation build-out as of 4 August 2026 [8]. We have flagged every item in this report by its “as of” date and recommend the reader treat Sections 6 and 7 as a living tracker rather than a static record.

title: Housing Access, Affordability, and Financialization in Italy: Evidence of Housing Market Exclusion from the Bank of Italy's Survey on Household Income and Wealth

detail.title: Housing Access, Affordability, and Financialization in Italy: Evidence of Housing Market Exclusion from the Bank of Italy's Survey on Household Income and Wealth
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the Italian housing market with the aim of analyzing tenure distribution and assessing the efficiency of the market. Using microdata provided by the Bank of Italy from the Survey on Household Income and Wealth, the study examines whether tenure distribution differs across regions and household types. While acknowledging that tenure outcomes are influenced by several determinants, the primary objective is to understand how the housing market is structured and stratified. The Italian housing market can be broadly described in terms of two main groups: homeowners and tenants. However, the analysis also identifies additional relevant categories, such as multiowners (families who possess more than one property) and landlords (families who rent at least one property they own). The presence and intensity of these groups provide important insights into the functioning and efficiency of the housing market. Furthermore, housing dynamics cannot be separated from financial market processes. This paper explores the extent to which financial mechanisms are embedded in the housing market, arguing that a higher degree of integration corresponds to a greater level of financialization, defined as the increasing influence of investment and speculative motives over fundamental housing needs. In this context, speculative dynamics are driven by the expected returns associated with rental income. These elements allow for the identification of two interconnected segments: the homeownership sector and the rental sector. Their interaction creates a situation in which property owners can extract additional income through the rental market, while tenants face limited bargaining power. From this perspective, it becomes difficult to interpret renting as a voluntary choice. On the contrary, the evidence presented in this study suggests that tenancy is largely the result of exclusionary mechanisms within the housing market. Empirically, the analysis is based on logistic and linear regression models, predictive probabilities and housing burden and financialization indicators, in order to capture both distributional patterns and the role of financial factors in shaping the Italian housing system.

title: Pro-Metrix Architecture: Formulation of an Original Framework Based on the Synthesis of Productivity Tools, Techniques, and Methods (TTM) in Corporate or Industrial Productivity Transformation

detail.title: Pro-Metrix Architecture: Formulation of an Original Framework Based on the Synthesis of Productivity Tools, Techniques, and Methods (TTM) in Corporate or Industrial Productivity Transformation
detail.abstract: This study formulates PRO-METRIX (Productivity Measurement & Transformation Matrix), an original framework that synthesizes a catalog of 64 productivity Tools, Techniques, and Methods (TTM)—previously compiled by the author in “The Application of TTM for Productivity Improvement” (Panjaitan, 2026a) — into a single two-axis matrix architecture: the 4P framework (People, Process, Product, Policy) and the Planning-Executing-Sustaining cycle (APO-PS 101:2023). This study specifically positions PRO-METRIX not as a competitor, but as a Tier-2 (deep-dive) instrument activated after the Tier-1 (screening)—exemplified by the PROFITO Framework v1.0 from the Special Region of Yogyakarta’s Department of Manpower and Transmigration—to identify high-risk companies, those in critical sectors, or those exhibiting significant anomalies. Four core modules were formulated as functional counterparts to the four PROFITO outputs: the Transformation Synergy Index (IST, derived from its Indonesian name “Indeks Sinergi Transformasi”), which integrates the Green Risk-Adjusted Productivity Index (GRAPI-N) as an assessment engine for physical resource efficiency; the Dynamic 4P Maturity Quadrant, which replaces the 1–5 ladder model with a multidimensional radar visualization; the Root Cause Navigation System (SNAM, derived from its Indonesian name Sistem Navigasi Akar Masalah), which automatically maps gaps to specific TTM tools; and the Execution & Financial Validation Blueprint, which integrates real-world technical-financial feasibility studies, exemplified through simulations of industrial wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) and building HVAC/AC energy efficiency audits. This study concludes that a two-tier architecture (Tier-1 screening – Tier-2 deep-dive) provides a stronger methodological foundation that is more readily accepted both academically and institutionally compared to a head-to-head competition model, while also providing a concrete pathway to guide a company’s green business transformation within the policy horizons of regional and national productivity initiatives.

title: After American Primacy -The End of American "Exceptionalism" Iran, The Yuan and the Transfer of Global Power Special Case Study: Canada's Role, A Swot Analysis and it’s Best Positioning to Adapt
affiliations: Szymon Zephan Capital (SZC Group)

detail.title: After American Primacy -The End of American "Exceptionalism" Iran, The Yuan and the Transfer of Global Power Special Case Study: Canada's Role, A Swot Analysis and it’s Best Positioning to Adapt
detail.abstract: American primacy rested on more than the size of the United States economy or the depth of the Treasury market. It joined five promises into a single operating system: the United States would protect critical sea lanes, provide a vast market, police a dollar-centred financial network, supply liquid safe assets, and impose costs on states that challenged the order. The 2026 Iran war did not instantly replace the dollar. It did something more consequential at the level of expectations: it separated those promises. Washington remained militarily formidable, yet it did not promptly restore normal passage through the Strait of Hormuz; its regional bases proved vulnerable; high-end munitions were consumed at rates that affected wider readiness; and negotiations increasingly concerned the terms of Iranian influence over the very chokepoint the campaign was meant to secure. This report argues that the end of American "exceptionalism" should be understood as the end of automaticity. Other states no longer assume that U.S. protection will be decisive, that access to U.S. markets will remain unconditional, that financial sanctions will compel rather than merely punish, or that alignment with Washington will be costless. The immediate result is not a clean succession from dollar to yuan. It is a layered transfer of power: trade routes and settlement practices change first; credit, hedging and custody follow; reserve portfolios adjust last. The yuan's central weakness-limited convertibility and a thinner safe-asset complex-remains real. Its strategic advantage is different: China can combine market access, manufacturing scale, energy demand, bilateral finance and alternative settlement with the demonstrated capacity of partner states to resist U.S. coercion. Canada is the report's special case because it is simultaneously the United States' closest economic partner, a beneficiary of the old order, a G7 power with resources desired by every major bloc, and a middle power newly compelled to hedge. Canada's best position is neither reflexive anti-Americanism nor passive continental dependence. It is allied strategic autonomy: preserve the irreplaceable benefits of North American integration while building European defence-industrial depth, Indo-Pacific and Gulf market options, tidewater energy and critical-mineral corridors, financial-contingency capacity, and a diplomatic role capable of working across rival systems.

title: Source Sovereignty: A Continental Framework for Taxing Value Where It Is Created in Africa

detail.title: Source Sovereignty: A Continental Framework for Taxing Value Where It Is Created in Africa
detail.abstract:
In this paper, I develop and quantify the Source Sovereignty Framework (SSF), which presents a continental policy architecture enabling African states to act as a coordinated bloc of 54 jurisdictions. This framework proposes that these states tax cross-border income precisely at the point of generation. This taxation is envisioned to be collected through gross-basis withholding mechanisms integrated within African payment systems, thereby rendering it independent of the consent, ratification, or administrative cooperation of capital-exporting states.

The SSF comprises five integral components: a core source-taxation principle; a four-layer legal architecture anchored in an African Union convention that binds African states to one another; a moderate gross-basis rate structure; a coordinated four-phase transition away from the existing bilateral treaty network; and an anti-defection mechanism aimed at preventing intra-African arbitrage.

Drawing on peer-reviewed literature concerning profit shifting, tax treaties, investment incentives, and digital taxation, I argue that the predominant objections to unilateral assertiveness by African nations, namely concerns regarding investor flight, double taxation, retaliation, and administrative incapacity, are either unsupported by empirical evidence or are adequately addressed by the design of the framework itself. Moreover, the UN Framework Convention on International Tax Cooperation, while diplomatically significant, cannot effectively substitute for a collection architecture that is deemed necessary to remain under African control.

Using a transparent scenario model, I predict that a fully phased-in SSF could yield incremental revenue of approximately US$20 billion annually by 2030 (US$11–33 billion) and around US$36 billion annually by 2035 (US$19–58 billion). Furthermore, I estimate that the cumulative financial gains over the period from 2028 to 2035 could reach approximately US$184 billion under central assumptions.

title: Xhdfe: Fast High-Dimensional Fixed-Effects Estimation in Stata
