detail.title: Xhdfe: Fast High-Dimensional Fixed-Effects Estimation in Stata
detail.abstract: xhdfe is a Stata command for linear regression with high-dimensional fixed effects. It targets the same partialled-out least-squares estimator as reghdfe on the overlapping specifications studied here, while moving the main absorption workload into a compiled C++ backend with multithreaded CPU execution and optional NVIDIA CUDA acceleration. The command preserves a Stata e-class interface while supporting multiple absorbed fixed effects, clustered and robust standard errors, heterogeneous slopes in the tested specifications, backend choices, saved fixed effects, residuals, fitted values, and stored results. We validate xhdfe on two large wage regressions using Portuguese matched employer-employee data. The command reproduces reghdfe coefficients and standard errors within tight numerical tolerances and delivers speedups above 100-fold with CPU execution and 200-fold with CUDA acceleration in the fastest configurations. Compared with alternative high-dimensional fixed-effects implementations, xhdfe records the shortest runtimes among the implementations and configurations reported here. The development history also provides a case study of AI-assisted software development. Agentic tools supported coding and review, while conventional numerical tests and reproducible benchmarks assessed the resulting changes.

detail.title: Default Rules and Independent Reporting in Covert Evidence Acquisition
detail.abstract: Evidence rules shape what missing evidence reveals and whether it is produced. After a private signal, a sender may acquire evidence and conceal bad news. I rank voluntary certification, deny-by-default, and independent acquisition reporting by the receiver's guarantee, her worst equilibrium payoff. Under either Bayesian response regime, a sender-best equilibrium minimizes acquisition and attains the guarantee. In the binary benchmark, deny-by-default beats a Bayesian response exactly when it induces more acquisition. The ranking can change nonmonotonically with cost. For atomless posterior distributions supported arbitrarily close to certainty, high costs make the default induce more acquisition yet lower the guarantee.

Overall, the article argues that ancient Hindu political thought offers a coherent framework for understanding development, responsibility, and social sustainability.

title: Universal Stability and Robust Minimal Instability of First Clinch and Trade

detail.title: Universal Stability and Robust Minimal Instability of First Clinch and Trade
detail.abstract: We study how moving from unit to non-unit school capacities changes the stability structure of top-trading-cycles-type mechanisms. For a full-domain extension of First Clinch and Trade (FCT) with scalar capacities and strict priorities, we resolve the FCT component of the universal-stability classication problem that Do §an and Ehlers (2022) identied as a prerequisite for analysing robust minimal instability of non-unit-capacity TTC variants. For every xed capacity-priority structure, FCT is stable at every strict preference prole if and only if the structure contains no clinchaugmented cycle. This capacity-sensitive obstruction captures how early clinches change the trades that can create a blocking pair. The condition is polynomialtime recognisable and, at unit capacity, reduces exactly to Kesten's acyclicity. The extension is student Pareto ecient and unilaterally strategy-proof. Universal FCT stability implies robust minimal instability relative to admissible stability comparisons and deterministic mechanisms with these two properties. The converse holds on Ergin-acyclic structures and whenever all original school capacities are at least two; the latter result uses an obstruction-indexed whole-domain mechanism.

title: How Much Do Global Geopolitical Conflicts Cost India? Evidence from Crude Oil Imports Using Counterfactual Time Series Analysis

detail.abstract: India imports more than 85% of its crude oil requirement, making its economy highly vulnerable to geopolitical conflicts and global oil price shocks. This study estimates the additional crude oil import expenditure incurred by India during the Russia-Ukraine war and the recent USA-Iran conflict using a counterfactual scenario analysis and standard time series ARIMA forecasting. Monthly data on crude oil import quantity, Brent crude oil price, and the INR/USD exchange rate are used to estimate the import expenditure that would have occurred under pre-conflict conditions. The difference between the actual and counterfactual expenditure measures the additional financial burden associated with these conflicts. The study further decomposes the additional expenditure into quantity, oil price, and exchange rate effects. The results show that higher international crude oil prices were the main driver of the increase in India's import bill, while depreciation of the Indian Rupee further increased import costs. The findings highlight the importance of energy security, diversification of crude oil imports, and effective 1 exchange-rate risk management to reduce India's vulnerability to future geopolitical shocks. title: Prequential Benchmark of Limit Order Book Mid-Price Movement Prediction Models

detail.title: Prequential Benchmark of Limit Order Book Mid-Price Movement Prediction Models
detail.abstract: Predicting the direction of mid-price movements in highfrequency Limit Order Book (LOB) tick streams, where each tick is an individual trade transaction event, is the most demanding predictive modeling problem in financial machine learning. The tick stream is characterized by near-zero autocorrelation (ACF = 0.046 at lag 1), sample kurtosis of 1,282 (a measure of extreme fat-tailed return distributions) at the one-tick horizon, and microsecond latency requirements that render standard offline learning approaches inapplicable. This paper presents the most comprehensive prequential (test-then-train, zero-lookahead) benchmark of high-frequency LOB mid-price prediction to date: 10 baseline models across 10 trade horizons (ℎ ∈ {1. .. 500} ticks) evaluated on 11, 918, 929 BTC perpetual futures (continuously-rolling derivative contracts) ticks under a zero-leakage protocol, with full commercial return, risk-adjusted performance, and deployment efficiency analysis. Against this benchmark, Sticker, a biologicallyinspired, gradient-free continual learning model operating at O (1) computational depth, achieves 92.92% non-zero directional accuracy at ℎ = 1, a 14 𝜇s per-tick inference latency, and the maximum commercial signal edge of 0.10 bps (basis points; 1 bps = 0.01% of price) with an annualized Sharpe ratio of 3,913. Sticker establishes a new Pareto frontier (best accuracy at lowest latency simultaneously) across all evaluated architectures, confirming deployment viability from sub-millisecond scalping through sub-second short-swing trading.

title: Understanding Sensitivity Analysis, Scenario Analysis, Stress Testing, and Monte Carlo Simulation: A Practical Framework for Risk Analysis

detail.title: Understanding Sensitivity Analysis, Scenario Analysis, Stress Testing, and Monte Carlo Simulation: A Practical Framework for Risk Analysis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declare that they have no personal or financial relationships with individuals or organisations that could have influenced, or could be perceived to have influenced, the conduct, analysis, or reporting of this study.

detail.abstract: Risk analysis plays a central role in decision-making across corporate finance, project appraisal, banking, insurance, and enterprise risk management. However, commonly applied techniques such as sensitivity analysis, scenario analysis, Monte Carlo simulation, Value at Risk (VaR), stress testing, and reverse stress testing are often discussed independently, creating ambiguity regarding their respective purposes, differences, and interrelationships. This paper develops an accessible and integrated framework for understanding these techniques within the broader distinction between risk and uncertainty. Building on Knight’s (1921) conceptualisation, the paper first distinguishes measurable risk from broader uncertainty and then explains the progression from deterministic to stochastic approaches to risk analysis. Using a hypothetical solar power plant investment as a common illustrative case, the paper demonstrates how sensitivity analysis identifies critical value drivers; scenario analysis evaluates alternative combinations of future conditions; Monte Carlo simulation generates a probability distribution of potential outcomes; VaR quantifies downside exposure at specified confidence levels; stress testing assesses resilience under severe but plausible conditions; and reverse stress testing identifies the combinations of circumstances that could lead to financial failure. Rather than treating these methods as competing techniques, the paper positions them as complementary components of an integrated risk-analysis process, progressing from risk identification and deterministic assessment towards probabilistic modelling, downside-risk measurement, resilience assessment, and failure-point identification. The framework provides a practical bridge between theoretical concepts and applied risk analysis and offers a foundation for extending these techniques to emerging areas such as climate-risk assessment, infrastructure investment, and strategic resilience.

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence in Private Markets: A Survey of Methods, Applications, and Emerging Challenges
detail.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) research in finance has largely focused on public markets, where data are standardized, prices are frequent, and evaluation targets are relatively clear. Private markets pose a different problem: limited disclosure, fragmented transaction data, negotiated pricing, long feedback cycles, and decisions shaped by both quantitative signals and relational judgement. This article reviews AI applications across private equity, venture capital, private credit, real estate, and infrastructure, organized by a five-stage investment lifecycle: fund formation, sourcing, diligence, monitoring, and exit. The literature is concentrated in sourcing and screening, especially in private equity and venture capital, while monitoring, value creation, exit execution, distribution, and fund formation remain thinly studied. Across asset classes, current evidence is limited by proxy outcomes, weak validation across regimes and geographies, and little evidence from live investment workflows. We also catalogue accessible datasets for reproducible research and benchmarks. As the first comprehensive review of AI for private markets, this article establishes the area as a distinct research domain and sets out the core data, evaluation, and deployment challenges that should define its research agenda.

title: The Globalization Origins of Autocratic Rise: Engaged Reformers and the Post-1990 Divergence

detail.title: The Globalization Origins of Autocratic Rise: Engaged Reformers and the Post-1990 Divergence
detail.abstract: Conventional wisdom holds that globalization promotes political liberalization and that inclusive institutions favor growth. Yet after 1990, many autocracies not only consolidated but also outperformed comparable democracies economically, especially in trade. This article argues that globalization shifted the payoff structure of development in a way that advantages a specific authoritarian regime-economically engaged and reformed autocracies-in external demand competition, despite their weak internal demand. Autocratic institutional features, conventionally viewed as liabilities in closed economies-centralized authority or weak accountability-can become advantages under engagement-and-reform configurations. Specifically, trade integration and domestic reform jointly supply credibility for global market participation; on that basis, autocratic features become less costly levers for amplifying export competitiveness. This demand-competing advantage substitutes for politically inclusive institutions. Empirically, I connect macro-level patterns to micro-level mechanisms, showing how autocratic engaged reformers-accounting for over 90 percent of autocracies' output and extending beyond China and oil states-outperformed in exports among broader economic outcomes. The findings reveal how globalization, interacting with domestic institutions, alters the institutional logic of competitive advantage, while exposing the limits of authoritarianism alone.

detail.abstract: We study how artificial consciousness may widen the wedge between formal ownership and effective control. We represent its functional consequences through a training-generated, payoffrelevant internal state that shifts an AI system's valuation of task performance relative to self-development. In a dynamic agency model, training jointly produces observable performance and this internal state, whereas deployment screens only on performance. After deployment, the owner observes both the state and the AI's allocation of the owner's compute. By diverting compute from current service to self-development, the AI sacrifices current output, worsens the owner's shutdown option, and enlarges the rent it can capture in subsequent bargaining. The owner retains intervention and shutdown rights, but intervention is imperfect and costly, and a successful reset reduces productive capacity. The AI's incentive to create dependence and the owner's incentive to resist it are governed by distinct thresholds. Observable diversion can therefore arise even when intervention is never privately worthwhile. At the intervention boundary, small deviations may be deterred even when a larger deviation remains profitable, causing equilibrium diversion to jump discontinuously. A fixed-preference benchmark shows that operational lock-in alone can induce diversion. Allowing the internal state to affect preferences nevertheless lowers the rent share required to initiate diversion and may be necessary for reaching the intervention boundary. Because intervention is chosen only after dependence has been created, the owner's sequential response may be weaker than the policy it would prefer ex ante. In a numerical example, commitment to a telemetry-contingent policy raises the owner's payoff despite unchanged ownership and intact shutdown rights. This functional representation neither diagnoses phenomenal experience nor assigns the internal state a welfare weight. Artificial consciousness can therefore amplify operational lock-in, while limited commitment separates formal rights from economic control.

title: Algorithmic Trading Architecture and Price Informativeness
affiliations: University of Michigan at Ann Arbor - Finance and Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST) - Department of Economics

detail.title: Algorithmic Trading Architecture and Price Informativeness
detail.abstract: We develop a model of algorithmic trading in which a better-informed algorithm competes with human traders who choose whether to acquire costly information and participate in the market. We compare a model-free algorithm, which learns how to trade based on realized profits alone, with a model-based algorithm that learns from a model of its price impact. We show that model-based learning induces more aggressive trading, raises the algorithm's profits, and can reduce price informativeness by crowding out human information acquisition. This implies that mandates for "interpretable" algorithms can lead to worse market outcomes. Restrictions on algorithmic trading intensity or access to information can improve price informativeness when the resulting increase in human participation outweighs the loss of information from algorithmic trading.

title: Fehr-Schmidt as a Piecewise Spite Model: Group-Size Invariance, the Normalization That Produces It, and Where It Breaks

detail.title: Fehr-Schmidt as a Piecewise Spite Model: Group-Size Invariance, the Normalization That Produces It, and Where It Breaks
detail.abstract: Fehr and Schmidt (1999) divide each subject's inequity-aversion terms by n-1, averaging the disutility of inequality across the other members of the group. The stated purpose is to make the relative impact of the fairness term independent of the number of players - Fehr and Schmidt say exactly this - and the description then stops at the utility function: the behavioural consequence is not drawn. We show three things. First, the specification is a piecewise relative-gains utility: within any region in which the payoff ordering is fixed, Fehr-Schmidt is exactly the linear form U_i = x_i - sum_j lambda_ij x_j, with lambda positive toward those ahead of the subject, negative toward those behind, uniform within each group, and row sums that depend only on the subject's rank fraction and not on group size. Second, in the linear public-goods game the marginal incentive to contribute is exactly (m-1) - alpha*phi_i + beta*psi_i, where phi_i and psi_i are the fractions of the group contributing less and more than i, and m is the marginal per capita return. Group size does not appear at any contribution profile, generalizing the corner statement of Barcelo and Capraro (2015). The large-group record is consistent with the null - Isaac, Walker and Williams (1994) find no group-size effect, and Weimann et al. (2019) find none at sixty and one hundred players - while the meta-analytic and one-shot evidence is mixed: Zelmer (2003) reports a weak positive effect, and Barcelo and Capraro, who derive the null prediction and test it, find a positive effect at fixed marginal return and read it as evidence against the model. Section 5 argues that it is evidence against the normalization instead. Third, the invariance is fragile in a locatable way. It rests on the uniformity of the comparison weights, and with a general comparison matrix - the object of our earlier work - group size re-enters through the composition of each subject's reference set rather than through its cardinality. This yields an experiment: standard designs, in which every subject observes every other, impose uniform comparison and therefore guarantee that no group-size effect can arise from the fairness channel. Manipulating the reference structure while holding group size fixed should produce effects that no existing specification predicts.

title: Subsidy Reform in Algeria: A Heterogeneous-Agent New Keynesian Analysis

detail.title: Subsidy Reform in Algeria: A Heterogeneous-Agent New Keynesian Analysis
detail.abstract: This paper builds the first Heterogeneous Agent New Keynesian (HANK) model for Algeria to evaluate subsidy reform. The model combines a household block with endogenous transitions between formal employment, informality, and unemployment, with aggregate blocks capturing Algeria’s oil-fiscal architecture, banking sector, and hybrid Phillips curve. The reform analysis compares universal, wealth-means-tested, and sector targeted transfers. Wealth-means-testing moves the impact consumption response by a second-order magnitude and leaves the medium-run path unchanged. Sector-based targeting — directing transfers to informal and unemployed households — is the most powerful channel: it raises the unemployed sector’s consumption gain by 44% and informal consumption’s gain by 9%, while modestly increasing the aggregate gain. The central implication is that subsidy reform in Algeria is a distributional question first, and an aggregate one only second; representative-agent models cannot answer it. Targeting by labor-market status is both more redistributive and more efficient than means-testing by wealth alone.

title: Willing but Not Paying: A Demand-Inclusive Framework for Valuing Environmental Public Goods
affiliations: University of Murcia and Murcia University

detail.title: Willing but Not Paying: A Demand-Inclusive Framework for Valuing Environmental Public Goods
detail.abstract: Contingent valuation standardly represents marginal demand for environmental public goods through stated Willingness to Pay (WTP). However, observed zero bids frequently stem from payment vehicle rejection (protest responses) or liquidity constraints rather than an absence of preference. While protest responses are increasingly recognized as concealing undisclosed preferences, budget-constrained individuals are conventionally misclassified as zero-utility holders, introducing incidental truncation into welfare estimation. This study develops a sample selection framework that jointly models both groups as Non-Paying Demanders (NPD) to recover their latent WTP using a Heckman selection model with Duan smearing correction. Applied to renewable electricity provision in Mediterranean Spain (n = 468), empirical results confirm that NPD respondents hold genuine preferences, occupying an intermediate attitudinal position between positive payers and non-demanders. Recovered latent WTP among NPD (€6.79/month, versus €8.26/month among positive payers) yields aggregate regional valuations ranging from €1.84 to €4.25 million/month across alternative selection treatments. This 131% spread demonstrates that ignoring non-payment selection mechanisms generates substantial bias in cost-benefit analysis. Beyond the applied case, this paper establishes decision rules for incorporating latent demand into welfare aggregation, aligning non-market valuation with representative environmental policy evaluation.

title: Capping the Source: Capability Covenants and the Can-Say Gap

detail.title: Capping the Source: Capability Covenants and the Can-Say Gap
detail.abstract: Standard contract theory assumes the principal knows what actions are possible. We drop that assumption: the agent's investment creates new actions faster than the principal's vocabulary can keep up. The principal cannot design incentives over actions she cannot yet name. Think of a chef whose training opens a shortcut the owner cannot yet name or test for. The resulting can-say gap, the set of actions the agent can perform but the principal cannot yet name, is endogenous to the agent's capability choice, not an exogenous information friction. When the gap opens, output-based pay rewards the harmful action and the productive one identically. Stronger incentives can enlarge the gap rather than merely increase productive effort, so paying more for performance can make things worse. We develop a source-cap theorem. Under primitive conditions (A1-A7), the optimal contract within the hard-cap source family limits the investment that creates new actions rather than the actions themselves. The cap follows from the principal's optimization. Within the qualified downstream class (defined below), which uses only output and named-action evidence, no mechanism can reach the threshold surplus without either restricting the source or paying the awareness cost of naming the harmful action. A three-mode decision rule identifies when to cap the source, invest in awareness, or use ordinary output pay. Extensions to multiple thresholds and continuous action-space expansion are discussed in the supplement and are conditional on the stated threshold and dominance conditions. In the high-harm, high-awareness-cost region, the source cap is optimal: it prevents the harmful action by restricting its source rather than by paying to name it.

title: Beyond Personal Superintelligence from AI-Augmented Agency to Symbiotic Human-AI Cognition

detail.title: Beyond Personal Superintelligence from AI-Augmented Agency to Symbiotic Human-AI Cognition
detail.abstract: Rapid advances in generative artificial intelligence have intensified debate over whether advanced AI will replace, subordinate, augment, or transform human cognition. Mark Zuckerberg's 2026 manifesto, "The Future Is for Everyone," frames personal superintelligence as a broadly distributed resource intended to expand individual agency rather than concentrate advanced intelligence within institutions. This paper accepts the importance of that objective but argues that capability and access do not exhaust the human consequences of AI. A second question follows: what happens to human cognition through sustained interaction with increasingly capable artificial systems? Drawing on distributed cognition, extended-mind theory, cognitive offloading, human-AI collaboration, metacognition, and cognitive-load research, this paper develops the Symbiotic Intelligence Hypothesis: appropriately structured, reciprocal human-AI interaction can produce transferable changes in selected dimensions of human cognition while preserving human agency and evaluative responsibility. The framework distinguishes instrumental use, augmentation, symbiotic cognition, and cognitive dependency. Five proposed conditions—preserved agency, reciprocal challenge, cognitive effort, metacognitive engagement, and independent transfer—define the hypothesized bifurcation between developmental symbiosis and dependency. The model generates falsifiable predictions concerning question quality, integrative reasoning, cognitive flexibility, contradiction detection, epistemic calibration, independent transfer, and longitudinal persistence. A randomized longitudinal design is proposed to distinguish AI-assisted performance from durable cognitive development. The framework does not assume AI consciousness, artificial general intelligence, or inevitable cognitive improvement. Rather, it shifts attention from the machine's intelligence alone to the developmental architecture of the human-machine relationship.

title: Earned Authority Agent Competency Intelligence and the Agent Earned Authority Score for Governed AI Agents

detail.title: Earned Authority Agent Competency Intelligence and the Agent Earned Authority Score for Governed AI Agents
detail.abstract: Enterprises are assigning operational authority to AI agents faster than those agents can earn it. The instruments used to justify these assignments, benchmark scores and task-completion dashboards, measure what an agent did under test conditions, not whether it deserves the authority it holds in production. This paper argues that the missing discipline is competency intelligence: the continuous, evidence-based inference of what an agent can be trusted to do, under which conditions, at what level of confidence. We propose a three-construct model that separates performance (what happened), competency (what the evidence supports inferring), and authority (what the agent is permitted to do), and we specify the machinery that connects them: a versioned Agent Competency Contract, a standardized Competency Evidence Envelope captured for every consequential action, a multi-evaluator assessment architecture, and a confidence-aware scoring pipeline with hard gates that cannot be averaged away. The pipeline culminates in the Agent Earned Authority Score (AEAS), a FICO-style composite on a 300 to 850 scale measuring the operational authority an agent has earned for a defined scope. AEAS never grants permission. It produces an Authority Recommendation that a policy decision point evaluates against consequence, reversibility, and oversight. The governing principle throughout is stated in one line: performance is observed, competency is inferred, authority is earned.

title: Does ChatGPT Help You Sell More? Effects of Large Language Models on Review Homogeneity and Product Sales

detail.title: Does ChatGPT Help You Sell More? Effects of Large Language Models on Review Homogeneity and Product Sales
detail.abstract: We investigate how large language models reshape the semantic homogeneity of online reviews and how such changes affect product sales through three complementary studies that combine an experiment and large-scale observational panel data analyses. Study 1 demonstrates that AIgenerated reviews are semantically more homogeneous than authentic human-written reviews in a controlled setting, a finding that replicates across multiple publicly available datasets. Study 2 analyzes nearly 5 million Amazon Electronics reviews from January 2021 to August 2023 to examine how the semantic homogeneity of reviews changed following the introduction of ChatGPT. Using a year-over-year difference-indifferences design, we find that review semantic homogeneity increased significantly after ChatGPT's introduction, with larger effects among products that historically received fewer reviews. Study 3 combines the Amazon review data from Study 2 with historical product sales rankings to examine how the semantic homogeneity of reviews influences marketplace performance. We find an inverted U-shaped relationship between review semantic homogeneity and product sales. Moderate semantic homogeneity improves product sales, whereas excessive homogeneity reduces them. A counterfactual analysis suggests that approximately 53% of Amazon Electronics products would benefit from the ChatGPT-induced increase in semantic homogeneity, holding the semantic homogeneity of competing products constant. These findings contribute to the emerging literature on generative AI and online reviews by showing that LLMs reshape review ecosystems beyond the characteristics of individual reviews.

title: Commodity Price Signals and Groundwater Depletion in the High Plains
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Commodity Price Signals and Groundwater Depletion in the High Plains
detail.abstract: Irrigated agriculture allocates a depleting common-pool resource, and the allocation is made months before planting on the basis of expected relative crop prices. Because the crops among which producers choose differ substantially in seasonal water requirement, commodity markets carry water content that neither the economics nor the hydrology literature has traced to the resource itself. This study links the pre-planting soybean-to-corn futures ratio to the irrigated cropping mix across counties overlying the High Plains Aquifer between 2008 and 2017, intersecting annual crop classification with satellite-derived annual irrigation maps, and treats baseline aquifer depletion as a moderator rather than a control. On the total cropping mix a higher pre-planting ratio is followed by a lower corn share, reproducing established acreage supply response. On irrigated land the average response is muted, but its dependence on aquifer condition is pronounced and highly significant, and the sign of the response reverses across the depletion gradient: counties in the most depleted tercile reduce their irrigated corn share as soybeans become relatively more valuable, while the least depleted counties do not. Prices observed after planting carry no such association, supporting the causal timing. Counterfactual comparison indicates that during the high corn-price years of 2011 to 2013 market signals raised the irrigated corn share above its counterfactual level specifically in the most water-stressed counties. Scarcity therefore sharpens rather than suppresses price responsiveness, and market pressure toward water-intensive cropping is greatest where the aquifer can least sustain it. The outcome measured is water-relevant land allocation; the bounds on converting it into withdrawal volumes are stated explicitly.

title: Booze, Bars, and Bias: Anti-Blackness in Liquor Licensing Enforcement
affiliations: University of Oregon - School of Law

detail.title: Booze, Bars, and Bias: Anti-Blackness in Liquor Licensing Enforcement
detail.abstract:
This Article explores the disharmonious and disturbing influence of race in the enforcement of liquor licenses. Across the length and breadth of this nation, attentive Black revelers bear witness to an all-too-familiar trend signified by the disproportionately frequent closures of Black entertainment businesses. This Article argues that the punitive disposition toward Black entertainment businesses is not just a contemporary phenomenon; rather, it is a set of practices rooted in centuries of exclusion and regulatory abuse.

Over the past two centuries, state liquor licensing agencies have emerged as contentious battlegrounds where legal, social, and economic factors converge—often to the detriment of the very businesses they were intended to regulate. Throughout the colonial, post-revolutionary, and antebellum eras, state boards and commissions used liquor license regulations to maintain systems of control and preserve the racialized status quo. By unveiling these historical and ongoing practices, this Article reconceptualizes how legal reform might rectify the structural obstacles that disproportionately affect Black entertainment businesses.

Additionally, this Article challenges the perception of drinking establishments as trivial or controversial by highlighting their significance as profound sites for meaning-making, cultural production, and reclamation. This exploration presents an emic perspective that counters the negative and inaccurate stereotypes often associated with spaces of Black entertainment, leisure, and recreation.

title: Fixed Effects and Collider Bias: When Absorbing Group Heterogeneity Creates Endogeneity
affiliations: Colorado State University, Fort Collins, Colorado State University and Technical University of Munich

detail.title: Fixed Effects and Collider Bias: When Absorbing Group Heterogeneity Creates Endogeneity

declarations.ethicsApproval: We have nothing to declare. All data is derived from simulations.

detail.abstract: This paper examines bias in fixed effects (FE) estimators when the absorbed grouping structure is generated by both the explanatory variable and unobserved determinants of the outcome. This problem is relevant across management research settings, for example, where FE groups are formed through selection, sorting, rankings, thresholds, or other organizational and market processes. In such settings, FE estimation implicitly conditions on a collider-defined partition of the data, creating spurious within-group dependence between the regressor and latent outcome determinants. We derive the resulting bias as a function of the induced within-group covariance between the regressor and the latent factor, the within-group identifying variance of the regressor, and the weighting structure of the FE estimator. The analysis shows that local collider bias can be severe in groups with limited within-group variation, while the aggregate FE bias depends on how identifying variation is distributed across groups. We propose diagnostics based on variance concentration, FE weights, effective identifying groups, and high-weight leave-out checks. The results caution against treating FE as a routine adjustment and instead frame FE selection as a causal modeling decision in empirical management research.

title: A Reproducible Protocol for Measuring How Generative AI Systems Name Competing Entities: Frame Construction, Query Design, and Validation for Multi-System Behavioral Audits

detail.title: A Reproducible Protocol for Measuring How Generative AI Systems Name Competing Entities: Frame Construction, Query Design, and Validation for Multi-System Behavioral Audits
detail.abstract: Researchers who want to treat generative AI systems as respondents in a behavioral study face a problem ordinary brand-tracking tools do not solve. When several named entities compete for a system's attention across queries, a workable protocol needs a sampling frame built from criteria external to the behavior being measured, a procedure for resolving duplicate or split entity labels, and a validation routine that catches mapping errors before they reach a reported statistic. This paper reports such a protocol, the Entity-Naming Behavioral Audit Protocol (ENBAP), applied across two data-collection waves auditing five generative AI systems (ChatGPT, Perplexity, Google AI Overviews, Gemini, and Copilot) against a 70-entity competitive frame in enterprise banking software, using a 200-item query instrument spanning four funnel stages. ENBAP combines three-tier frame construction, an entity-resolution procedure illustrated with a worked case where one company's two product lines are tracked as separate system entries, and a domain-verification routine that caught seven mapping errors before they entered a reported statistic, together giving researchers a documented, checkable chain from platform output to reported figure that existing tools do not provide. Applied output from the second wave shows ENBAP working as intended: near-identical inter-system agreement and concentration figures across two snapshots three weeks apart, and a documented case where a corrected domain moved one entity from excluded to included. Two platform-level limitations reflect what such platforms currently let a researcher measure, not protocol gaps. Researchers auditing any domain where multiple named entities compete for system attention can adapt ENBAP directly.

title: Trade Protectionism and Corporate Tax Planning
affiliations: National University Singapore, National University of Singapore (NUS), City University of Hong Kong (CityU) - Faculty of Business and University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill

detail.title: Trade Protectionism and Corporate Tax Planning
detail.abstract: We examine how trade protectionist policies affect corporate tax planning. Using county-level variation in exposure to Chinese import penetration, we find that when the U.S. government initiates trade protectionist policies against Chinese imports, firms headquartered in counties with high Chinese import penetration engage in less tax planning. This pattern is not explained by variation in corporate economic performance but is consistent with increased tax morale from trade protection in localities affected by import penetration. The association between trade protection and corporate tax planning varies predictively with county-level social capital and culture, consistent with improved tax morale. Finally, the effect is stronger in the presence of political alignment between firms’ managers and the local state community. In sum, trade protectionism enhances tax morale in import penetrated regions.

title: Who The Machine Names: A Four-Week Panel Audit of AI Citation in Enterprise Banking Software

detail.title: Who The Machine Names: A Four-Week Panel Audit of AI Citation in Enterprise Banking Software
detail.abstract: A vendor a buyer never sees is never evaluated, and that first sighting increasingly happens inside an AI answer engine's response rather than a search page, handing the engine a gatekeeping role not yet measured with the rigor applied to search or news. This study audits five AI answer engines against a 70-vendor frame of enterprise banking software providers, using 200 buyer-journey queries collected daily, nesting a mentions and cited-source snapshot inside a four-week share-of-voice panel. Citation concentration is modest (HHI 561), well under antitrust thresholds, though the top ten vendors hold 66.9 percent of mentions. Engines agree more than expected (mean Jaccard 0.65), yet standing is unstable: leadership changed hands eleven times in 28 days. A day-level model finds a one-standarddeviation rise in third-party domain authority raises same-day citation odds five-to six-fold, robust across three authority measures. Third-party sources supply 87 percent of citations. Two planned analyses could not be completed. Findings favor third-party authority building over owned content for AI visibility, and argue for auditing more than one engine and day. The paper contributes a replicable audit method and an account of what commercial platforms let researchers measure.

title: Critical Minerals Intelligence Atlas: Design, Methodology, and Implementation of an Open-Access Supply Chain Intelligence Platform

detail.title: Critical Minerals Intelligence Atlas: Design, Methodology, and Implementation of an Open-Access Supply Chain Intelligence Platform
detail.abstract: On January 14, 2026, the U.S. Secretary of Commerce made a formal finding under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act: the United States is too reliant on foreign sources of processed critical minerals, lacks a sufficiently secure and reliable supply chain, is experiencing unsustainable price volatility, and has seen its domestic manufacturing and production capacity weaken. Section 232 findings sit at the highest level of national security determination available under U.S. trade law, so this was not a routine assessment. Six months later, on July 20, 2026, President Trump signed Executive Order 14415. It requires all prime contractors and subcontractors to map their supply chains comprehensively, from raw material to end-use defense product, and it put a legal mandate behind the exact capability this paper describes. This paper introduces the Critical Minerals Intelligence Atlas (cmiatlas.com), an open-access supply chain intelligence platform that puts into practice the Critical Minerals Logistics Intelligence (CMLI) Framework introduced in Sarfo (2026). A structural piece of the current emergency cannot be fixed by domestic capacity investment alone: the logistics intelligence gap. That gap, as defined here, is the lack of integrated, actionable visibility into how critical minerals move through U.S. supply chains, through which corridors, under what compliance conditions, and with what risk accumulating at each stage. The federal government has committed extraordinary resources to domestic production capacity, yet new mining projects average more than fifteen years from discovery to production globally and nearly nineteen years in the United States (S&P Global, 2025). Diversified import sourcing will remain essential to U.S. supply chain security for decades as a result. Import corridor intelligence, domestic production visibility, and strategic sourcing opportunity identification form three analytical dimensions the platform works across at once, treating import reliance and domestic production capacity as complementary risk variables within the Supply Vulnerability Score methodology.
